documents.title: Academic Affairs Guidance for Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools
documents.summary: Short university-wide statement from Academic Affairs, effective January 2024. Faculty decide whether and how generative AI is used in courses; if they say nothing, AI is permitted with disclosure. Everyone is the author of AI-produced content and must respect law, privacy and ethics.
documents.stance_why: The policy statement and principles say "Faculty should decide whether and how generative AI is used in courses", so the document does not set one stance but hands the decision to instructors. It gives a fallback ("permitted but must be disclosed") and general duties, but no tiers; the dominant move is delegation, so delegates.

units.why: The opening sentence calls AI "a valuable, dynamic, and vital tool", the university's general view of AI that frames the policy; it is a preamble principle (P56), not a rule on a specific use.
units.anchor: Artificial Intelligence is a valuable, dynamic, and vital tool.

units.why: "you must abide by all applicable laws and policies when you use AI" binds everyone and obliges them to follow existing law and policy, so P77 and must.
units.anchor: you must abide by all applicable laws and policies when you use AI
units.policy: Users must abide by all applicable laws and policies when they use AI.

units.why: "you should strive to use AI ethically" is a general call to ethical use with no specific content, which is P116; it is a soft "should".
units.anchor: you should strive to use AI ethically
units.policy: Users should strive to use AI ethically.

units.why: "follow guidelines (including prohibitions) provided by your dean, instructor, supervisor" tells people to follow the local rules that apply to them (P78); P04 is about who sets the rule, while this is the duty of the person bound.
units.anchor: You should follow guidelines (including prohibitions) provided by your dean, instructor, supervisor
units.policy: People should follow the guidelines, including prohibitions, provided by their dean, instructor, supervisor or other individual overseeing their work.
units.fit_note: Covers deans and supervisors as well as course instructors, and says prohibitions may be among the guidelines.

units.why: "You should disclose the use of AI in an appropriate way" asks all users to acknowledge AI use, with the form left open ("appropriate way"); P24 and a soft "should".
units.anchor: You should disclose the use of AI in an appropriate way.

units.why: "exercise sound judgment in your use of AI" is a general call for good judgment with no specific content, so P116 rather than P118, which requires weighing benefits and risks.
units.anchor: You should exercise sound judgment in your use of AI.

units.why: "consistent with university policies on confidentiality and privacy" tells users to keep AI use within privacy and confidentiality rules, which is P50 as a should.
units.anchor: consistent with university policies on confidentiality and privacy

units.why: "This applies to all aspects of research, service work, and creative expression" sets the scope of the statement beyond teaching; a scope statement for the framework (P56) rather than a rule on research AI (P62).
units.anchor: This applies to all aspects of research, service work, and creative expression.

units.why: "You are the author of content that you produce with AI and responsible for its accuracy" makes the user own and answer for the output, matching P29; the accuracy duty touches P31 but ownership is the main claim.
units.anchor: You are the author of content that you produce with AI and responsible for its
units.policy: The user is the author of content produced with AI and is responsible for its accuracy, impact, and compliance with relevant laws and policies.

units.why: "Faculty should decide whether and how generative AI is used in courses" puts the course-level decision with faculty rather than setting one rule, which is P04.
units.anchor: Faculty should decide whether and how generative AI is used in courses.

units.why: "Faculty should clearly communicate expectations to students" asks instructors to state their AI expectations, P09, although the sentence does not name the syllabus.
units.anchor: Faculty should clearly communicate expectations to students.
units.fit_note: Does not name the syllabus; says only to communicate expectations clearly.

units.why: "the use of such tools is permitted but must be disclosed" gives the fallback when no instructor statement exists: permitted with mandatory disclosure. P06 (fallback when silent), chosen over P24 because the point is the default.
units.anchor: the use of such tools is permitted but must be disclosed
units.policy: If an instructor does not provide a statement on generative AI tools, their use is permitted but must be disclosed.

units.why: "Faculty should clearly communicate what constitutes academic dishonesty" asks instructors to define misuse for their course; closest to P09, the definition of misconduct being part of the expectations.
units.anchor: Faculty should clearly communicate what constitutes academic dishonesty.
units.fit_note: Asks for communicating what counts as academic dishonesty, not AI permissions as such.

units.why: "Students are responsible for understanding the rules of engagement for using AI in each of their courses" places on students the duty to learn each course's AI rules, which is P78.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for understanding the rules of engagement for using AI

units.why: "seeking out information if they do not understand" tells students who are unsure to find out more; the P10 pattern (ask when unsure), though it does not name the instructor or say to refrain from using AI.
units.anchor: seeking out information if they do not understand
units.policy: Students seek out information if they do not understand the rules for using AI in a course.
units.fit_note: Says to seek out information, not specifically to ask the instructor before using AI.

units.why: "Faculty and students must disclose how and when AI is used in research, service work, reviews, data collection" is a must-disclose rule that reaches beyond coursework; P24 rather than P62 because it requires disclosure rather than setting research rules.
units.anchor: must disclose how and when AI is used in research
units.policy: Faculty and students must disclose how and when AI is used in research, service work, reviews, data collection, and creative expression.
units.fit_note: Covers research, service, reviews, data collection and creative work, not only course submissions.

units.why: "Faculty and students are the authors of content generated by AI and are responsible for that content" repeats ownership for both groups as a principle bullet; P29, kept separate because it is the principles list and names faculty too.
units.anchor: are the authors of content generated by AI and are responsible
units.policy: Faculty and students are the authors of content generated by AI and are responsible for that content as they are with content that they author.

units.why: "AI should be used in ways that respect confidentiality and privacy" is a principle bullet naming privacy; P50, with "should".
units.anchor: AI should be used in ways that respect confidentiality and privacy.

units.why: "AI should be used ethically and reasonably" is a general call for ethical and reasonable use with no specific content, which is P116.
units.anchor: AI should be used ethically and reasonably.

documents.title: Academic Integrity and Generative AI
documents.summary: Hub page that restates the university stance (instructors decide, default permit with disclosure) and gives advice on syllabus statements, discussing integrity with students and redesigning assignments. It explains why AI detectors are unreliable and sets the standards for Honor Council reports of unauthorized AI use.
documents.stance_why: The page says "The university empowers instructors to establish their own policies" and "If you do not provide a statement ... the university permits students to use generative AI tools, but they must disclose". No single stance is set; the page hands the decision to instructors and only supplies a fallback, so delegates.

units.why: The page opens by saying it is "reasonable to be concerned that your students may abuse or misuse these tools", framing its purpose and the problem; a preamble (P56) with no rule.
units.anchor: it is reasonable to be concerned that your students may abuse or misuse these tools

units.why: "The university empowers instructors to establish their own policies" gives instructors the authority to set AI rules, so P04; "empowers" makes it a permission (may).
units.anchor: The university empowers instructors to establish their own policies on the use of generative AI
units.policy: The university empowers instructors to establish their own policies on the use of generative AI in the classroom.

units.why: "within the guidelines of the Honor Code" says instructor AI policies must sit inside the existing Honor Code, i.e. comply with existing university policy (P77).
units.anchor: within the guidelines of the Honor Code
units.policy: Instructor policies on generative AI must stay within the guidelines of the Honor Code.

units.why: "It is your responsibility to determine how or if you allow your students to use these tools" assigns the allow-or-not decision to the instructor as a duty (must); P04, distinct from the empowerment sentence.
units.anchor: It is your responsibility to determine how or if you allow your students to use

units.why: "it is your responsibility to clearly communicate your expectations" when allowing AI requires instructors to state their expectations; P09 with must.
units.anchor: it is your responsibility to clearly communicate your expectations for how they engage

units.why: "even if you choose to completely prohibit ... you should state this policy clearly" extends the duty to communicate to instructors who ban AI; P09, with the point that a ban also needs stating.
units.anchor: even if you choose to completely prohibit the use of generative AI tools, you should
units.fit_note: Specifies that a complete prohibition must also be stated.

units.why: "the university permits students to use generative AI tools, but they must disclose all generative AI usage" is the university fallback when the syllabus is silent (P06); it also makes students disclose, but the fallback is the main point.
units.anchor: the university permits students to use generative AI tools, but they must disclose all generative
units.policy: If an instructor provides no statement on generative AI tools, the university permits students to use them but they must disclose all generative AI usage.

units.why: "For the university's official policy ... please visit this page" points readers to the Academic Affairs guidance, which is P115.
units.anchor: For the university’s official policy on the use of generative AI, please visit this page

units.why: "Including a statement in your syllabus can be a helpful way to clearly state your expectations" recommends a syllabus statement without requiring it; P09 as a "should".
units.anchor: Including a statement in your syllabus can be a helpful way to clearly state your
units.fit_note: Presents the syllabus statement as helpful, not mandatory.

units.why: The questions ask instructors to decide "For what purposes can students use these tools" such as brainstorming, proofreading or composing text; a prompt to set permitted uses per instructor (P04), not itself a rule on any use.
units.anchor: For what purposes can students use these tools

units.why: "How do I define appropriate and ethical usage for generative AI?" asks instructors to define appropriate use in their syllabus statement; P09, as a consideration.
units.anchor: How do I define appropriate and ethical usage for generative AI?

units.why: "What constitutes academic misconduct within my course with respect to the use of generative AI?" asks the instructor to define misconduct for their course; P09, as for the Academic Affairs guidance.
units.anchor: What constitutes academic misconduct within my course with respect to the use of generative AI?
units.fit_note: About defining misconduct rather than permissions.

units.why: "How will I ensure students are aware of and respect any applicable confidentiality and privacy policies?" asks instructors to address privacy in the AI statement; P50 as a prompt.
units.anchor: How will I ensure students are aware of and respect any applicable confidentiality and privacy

units.why: "How will I require students to disclose and/or cite their use of generative AI?" with APA or MLA options asks instructors to set a disclosure and citation rule; P24.
units.anchor: How will I require students to disclose and/or cite their use of generative AI?

units.why: "How will I ensure my students understand their responsibility for AI-generated content?" asks the instructor to make students accountable for AI output; P29.
units.anchor: How will I ensure my students understand their responsibility for AI-generated content?

units.why: "Are there assignments where my expectations differ from the guidelines presented at the beginning of the semester?" tells instructors that rules can vary by assignment and must be conveyed; P04 (per-assignment).
units.anchor: Are there assignments where my expectations differ from the guidelines presented at the beginning of

units.why: "see this handout on Sample Syllabi Statements" points instructors to sample syllabus language, which is P110.
units.anchor: see this handout on Sample Syllabi Statements for Generative AI and ChatGPT Usage

units.why: "you might also consider having a conversation with your students about generative AI tools at the beginning of the semester and throughout" goes beyond a syllabus line to class discussion, which is P66.
units.anchor: you might also consider having a conversation with your students about generative AI tools

units.why: "check out our resource on Incorporating Generative AI in the Classroom" directs instructors to another guide, which is P115.
units.anchor: check out our resource on Incorporating Generative AI in the Classroom

units.why: "Rather than simply relying on detection strategies, you may want to consider proactively addressing the use of generative AI and minimizing opportunities for the misuse" recommends prevention over detection; P99 fits best, though it speaks of opportunities, not pressures.
units.anchor: proactively addressing the use of generative AI and minimizing opportunities for the misuse of these
units.fit_note: Concerns minimizing opportunities for misuse, not easing pressures.

units.why: "Students are more likely to exhibit academic dishonesty if they do not understand the purpose of a policy ... or perceive that acting dishonestly is the norm" gives causes of cheating as the basis for an integrity culture; P99, the causes of misuse.
units.anchor: Students are more likely to exhibit academic dishonesty if they do not understand the purpose

units.why: "consider how you might develop a culture of academic integrity in your classroom" recommends building an integrity culture; the rationale is the community's integrity (P95) more than skill-building.
units.anchor: develop a culture of academic integrity in your classroom
units.fit_note: Advice to build an integrity culture, not a reason for a rule.

units.why: "sharing why academic integrity is important, involving students in conversations about integrity" asks instructors to discuss the reasons with students; P66.
units.anchor: involving students in conversations about integrity or inviting students to discuss

units.why: "remind students Vanderbilt has a unifying Honor Code across all schools" ties AI use to the Honor Code and its tradition; P95 (integrity culture) rather than P77 since the point is motivation.
units.anchor: Vanderbilt has a unifying Honor Code across all schools

units.why: "give students the opportunity to ask questions about both the policy itself and the reasons for the policy" asks instructors to explain the rationale and invite questions; P66.
units.anchor: give students the opportunity to ask questions about both the policy itself and the reasons

units.why: "setting clear expectations, providing support and scaffolding ... explaining the relevance of an activity and providing opportunities for growth" lists ways to motivate compliance by easing causes of misuse; P99.
units.anchor: setting clear expectations, providing support and scaffolding to complete activities

units.why: "connect students to resources that can help them succeed academically" such as coaching, tutoring and writing consultations points students to human support; P72.
units.anchor: connect students to resources that can help them succeed academically

units.why: "modifying existing assignments to discourage the use and abuse of generative AI tools" is a recommendation to redesign assignments around AI; P35.
units.anchor: modifying existing assignments to discourage the use and abuse of generative AI tools

units.why: "design opportunities for students to develop AI literacy by incorporating generative AI into your teaching" suggests teaching with AI to build literacy; P44 (teach effective AI use), as an option.
units.anchor: design opportunities for students to develop AI literacy by incorporating generative AI into your teaching
units.fit_note: Frames the aim as AI literacy, not employer expectation.

units.why: "consider whether your changes could inadvertently create new hurdles and burdens for students with disabilities" asks instructors to check accessibility when adapting assignments; P97.
units.anchor: could inadvertently create new hurdles and burdens for students with disabilities

units.why: "Requiring students to use information discussed in class, specific texts and other information that would not be readily available online" is the "Localize assignments" strategy; P35.
units.anchor: Requiring students to use information discussed in class, specific texts

units.why: "Asking students to reflect on their personal experiences and opinions can help distinguish AI-generated text" is the "Incorporate personal reflections" strategy; P35.
units.anchor: Asking students to reflect on their personal experiences and opinions

units.why: "Breaking an assignment down into several smaller tasks that build up to a final project can minimize the likelihood of students turning to generative AI" is the scaffolding strategy; P35.
units.anchor: Breaking an assignment down into several smaller tasks that build up to a final project

units.why: "Use exploratory and hands-on activities" is a strategy heading (its body repeats the scaffolding text); coded as P35 since it recommends activity redesign.
units.anchor: Use exploratory and hands-on activities

units.why: "Require analysis and critical thinking" because AI tools are "often less adept" at it recommends assignments that demand analysis; P35.
units.anchor: Require analysis and critical thinking

units.why: "consider having students complete these tasks in class" moves AI-prone tasks into class to prevent AI use, shifting weight toward unassisted work (P33).
units.anchor: consider having students complete these tasks in class

units.why: "There are currently no foolproof methods for detecting the use of generative AI" states that AI use cannot be verified reliably; P82.
units.anchor: There are currently no foolproof methods for detecting the use of generative AI.

units.why: "certain red flags that can indicate that a student may have used generative AI" followed by a list (inaccuracies, tone, citations, dead links) names kinds of evidence to weigh; P69.
units.anchor: there are certain red flags that can indicate that a student may have used generative
units.fit_note: Offers indicators rather than a standard of proof.

units.why: "Compare to previous work. A major change in tone and style from previous writings could indicate" use is a specific evidence type (comparison with prior work); P69.
units.anchor: A major change in tone and style from previous writings could indicate that a student

units.why: "Because generative AI tools frequently generate inaccurate information, a text with multiple errors or flagrant inaccuracies may be a sign" names AI-typical errors as evidence; P69.
units.anchor: a text with multiple errors or flagrant inaccuracies may be a sign that a student

units.why: "a single inaccuracy or a slight change in style may not necessarily mean that a student has used generative AI" sets a limit on inference from red flags: single signs are not enough; P69.
units.anchor: a single inaccuracy or a slight change in style may not necessarily mean

units.why: "traditional plagiarism checkers are not reliable sources of generative AI detection" says detectors cannot be relied on; P39.
units.anchor: traditional plagiarism checkers are not reliable sources of generative AI detection

units.why: "entering student data into these tools may violate student privacy protections such as FERPA" warns against putting student work into detectors; P50 (protect personal data), not P20 which concerns students.
units.anchor: entering student data into these tools may violate student privacy protections such as FERPA
units.policy: Entering student data into third-party AI detection tools may violate student privacy protections such as FERPA.

units.why: "Vanderbilt currently does not offer any institutionally supported AI detection tools" states the university does not provide a detector; P39 is closest, though this is a factual statement about provision.
units.anchor: Vanderbilt currently does not offer any institutionally supported AI detection tools
units.fit_note: Reports non-provision of detectors rather than telling instructors not to rely on them.

units.why: "Lack of public-facing, detailed methodologies" in detectors such as Turnitin is a reason detectors are untrustworthy; P39.
units.anchor: Lack of public-facing, detailed methodologies and standards for detecting AI-generated text.

units.why: "Bias against non-native English speakers" says detectors label their text as AI more often; a bias harm (P53), chosen over P39 because the sentence names bias as the harm.
units.anchor: Early studies suggest that generative AI detectors are more likely to label text written by
units.fit_note: Bias in detection tools rather than in generative AI.

units.why: "Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT cannot reliably detect unauthorized AI use" tells instructors not to use chatbots as detectors; P39.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT cannot reliably detect unauthorized AI use.

units.why: "Many generative AI Tools have ambiguous privacy policies and may not protect student information according to FERPA standards" warns about putting student work into chatbots; P50.
units.anchor: may not protect student information according to FERPA standards

units.why: "comparing a student's work to an AI-generated response to the assignment prompt does not yield reliable results" says a specific detection technique fails; P39.
units.anchor: comparing a student's work to an AI-generated response to the assignment prompt does not yield

units.why: "Depending on the strength of the suspicion, options include: Issuing a warning, Reporting to the respective honor council" gives graduated responses to suspected misuse; P81 (formal reporting procedure) with the warning option as part of it.
units.anchor: Depending on the strength of the suspicion, options include:
units.fit_note: Also gives issuing a warning as an alternative to reporting.

units.why: "a report to the Undergraduate Honor Council cannot be based solely on an artificial intelligence detector score" bars detector score as sole basis; P69 (evidence standard, broadened for detector output).
units.anchor: a report to the Undergraduate Honor Council cannot be based solely on an artificial intelligence

units.why: Reports "must meet the following standards" including alignment with the Academic Affairs policy and supporting factors such as fake links or style inconsistency; a required evidentiary standard, P69.
units.anchor: reports of unauthorized AI use to the Undergraduate Honor Council

units.why: The Honor Council asks "is it more likely than not" that unauthorized aid was given and "does not have to determine if AI usage occurred"; a standard of proof, P69.
units.anchor: is it more likely than not that this student gave and/or received unauthorized aid
units.policy: The Undergraduate Honor Council asks whether it is more likely than not that the student gave or received unauthorized aid on the assignment; it does not have to determine if AI usage occurred.

units.why: The council "will consider factors including" assignment instructions, syllabus policies, comparison with the full body of work, and testimony; kinds of evidence to weigh, P69.
units.anchor: will consider factors including (but not limited to):

units.why: The council "will not" consider "AI detection scores" among other factors, so detector scores are excluded as evidence; P69 (broadened) rather than P39 because it states what evidence counts in an integrity finding.
units.anchor: AI detection scores

units.why: "the panel will assign penalty based on the following factors: Flagrancy, Premeditation, Truthfulness" says how penalties are set but states no concrete penalty, so not P37; no other type covers the factors for sanctioning.
units.anchor: the panel will assign penalty based on the following factors:
units.uncovered_note: Penalties are set by the panel according to flagrancy, premeditation and truthfulness, with no fixed sanction named.

units.why: The resources list offers a "Warning letter template for faculty", a template for responding to suspected misuse; closest P110 (templates), though it is a letter template and not syllabus language.
units.anchor: Warning letter template for faculty
units.fit_note: A template for warning letters after suspected misuse, not syllabus language.

units.why: "Request training from the Student Care Network" is suggested for working with students distressed by an honor code accusation, directing to human support after an alleged violation; P72 closest, though support concerns accused students.
units.anchor: Request training from the Student Care Network
units.fit_note: Support is for students distressed by an honor code accusation.

notes: Coder A. Doc 1 text has a PDF break ('ar e'), kept verbatim in one anchor-adjacent fragment. The hub page's 'Use exploratory and hands-on activities' body repeats the scaffolding text; coded once as the heading.
